title: How do you bring existing (manually-created or legacy) AWS resources under Terraform management as a workflow — write the matching resource config → `terraform import` into state → `terraform plan` → iterate on the config until the plan proposes NO unexpected changes → commit — and why does importing into state NOT automatically produce correct/clean config (you still must author accurate HCL, strip noise, introduce variables/modules)?
shortTitle: Bringing existing/legacy AWS resources under Terraform management (write config → import → plan → iterate → commit), and why import alone does not produce clean config

s1_definition.profdef: `terraform import` binds an already-existing real-world infrastructure object to a Terraform resource address in the state file. It populates state only; it does not generate configuration. The correct adoption workflow is to first author HCL that matches the live resource, run `terraform import` to map the real object into state, run `terraform plan`, and then iterate on the HCL until the plan shows no changes, because a clean plan proves that your configuration and the real resource are in agreement.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India has an old safe-deposit vault that a contractor installed years ago without any paperwork. Terraform is the bank's official asset register. Importing is like writing the vault's serial number into the register so the bank now "knows" it owns the vault. But writing the serial number does NOT describe the vault — its size, lock type, and location. You still have to walk to the vault, measure it, and write an accurate description by hand. If your written description says "small vault" but the real vault is large, the next audit (the plan) will scream "mismatch." You keep fixing your description until the audit is silent.
s1_definition.oneliner: Import fills state, not config — you still hand-write accurate HCL until `terraform plan` shows zero drift.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `terraform import` binds an already-existing real-world infrastructure object to a Terraform resource address in the state file. It populates state only; it does not generate configuration. The correct adoption workflow is to first author HCL that matches the live resource, run `terraform import` to map the real object into state, run `terraform plan`, and then iterate on the HCL until the plan shows no changes, because a clean plan proves that your configuration and the real resource are in agreement.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India has an old safe-deposit vault that a contractor installed years ago without any paperwork. Terraform is the bank's official asset register. Importing is like writing the vault's serial number into the register so the bank now "knows" it owns the vault. But writing the serial number does NOT describe the vault — its size, lock type, and location. You still have to walk to the vault, measure it, and write an accurate description by hand. If your written description says "small vault" but the real vault is large, the next audit (the plan) will scream "mismatch." You keep fixing your description until the audit is silent.

**One line to remember:** Import fills state, not config — you still hand-write accurate HCL until `terraform plan` shows zero drift.

sections.s2_technical:
Terraform tracks three things: the configuration (your HCL files, the desired state), the state file (Terraform's record of what it manages), and the real infrastructure (what actually exists in AWS). A normal `terraform apply` keeps all three in sync. When a resource was created manually outside Terraform, the state file knows nothing about it, so Terraform would try to CREATE a duplicate if you naively wrote config and applied. Import solves exactly this: it writes a state entry that says "this Terraform address corresponds to this real AWS object."

The classic command form is `terraform import aws_s3_bucket.audit nbi-audit-logs-prod`, where `aws_s3_bucket.audit` is the resource address you must have already declared in HCL (even if it is an empty shell), and `nbi-audit-logs-prod` is the real bucket name AWS uses as its import ID. Each resource type documents its own import ID format — a bucket uses its name, an EC2 instance uses `i-0abc123`, a security group uses `sg-0abc123`, a route table association uses a compound ID.

Here is why import alone is never enough. Import reads the live attributes into state, but your HCL is still whatever you typed. If your HCL omits `versioning`, `server_side_encryption_configuration`, or `tags` that the real bucket has, the first plan will propose to REMOVE or CHANGE them, because Terraform believes your config is the desired truth. So you run `terraform plan`, read every single proposed change, and copy the real settings into your HCL until the plan is empty. This is the iterate loop. Newer Terraform (1.5+) adds an `import {}` block and `terraform plan -generate-config-out=generated.tf` which can scaffold HCL for you, but the generated HCL is noisy — it dumps every computed and default attribute — so you still must strip read-only fields, replace hardcoded values with `var.` references, and group resources into modules.

A senior nuance: never import straight into production state on your first attempt. Take a backup of the state (`terraform state pull > backup.tfstate`), import, and if the plan looks wrong you can `terraform state rm` the address to undo the mapping without touching the real resource. Import only edits state; it never mutates AWS.
sections.s3_banking:
At the National Bank of India, a security contractor manually created an S3 bucket called `nbi-audit-logs-prod` two years ago to store transaction audit logs for Rajesh's savings account SAV2001 and Priya's current account CUR3001. It has versioning on, AES-256 encryption, and a `team=compliance` tag. Nobody wrote Terraform for it. Now the platform team wants ALL infrastructure under Terraform so changes go through pull requests.

Problem 1 — The bucket exists but Terraform does not know about it. If an engineer writes `resource "aws_s3_bucket"` and runs apply, Terraform tries to CREATE a second bucket and fails because the name is globally taken, or worse, it would recreate and wipe audit history. This is exactly what import solves: we map the real bucket into state first.

Problem 2 — After import, the first plan wrongly wants to turn OFF versioning and encryption, because the engineer's HCL did not mention them. This is the "import does not write config" lesson. We must read the plan and hand-author the versioning and encryption blocks until the plan is clean.

Problem 3 — The raw config has the bucket name and region hardcoded. For reuse across environments we introduce variables. This is the "strip noise, introduce variables" step.

Our runnable Java simulation models this whole workflow as an in-memory engine: a `TerraformState` (what Terraform thinks it manages), a `LiveInfrastructure` (what AWS really has), and a `ConfiguredResource` (the HCL the engineer wrote). The `ImportEngine` has `importResource()` which copies the live ID into state WITHOUT copying attributes into config, and `plan()` which diffs config against live and reports proposed changes. We will see the plan complain, then we patch the config, then the plan goes clean.

The classes are: `LiveInfrastructure` (the real AWS bucket), `TerraformState` (managed addresses), `ConfiguredResource` (engineer's HCL), `ImportEngine` with `importResource()` and `plan()`, and a `TerraformImportDemo` main that runs the full import-plan-iterate loop and logs every step.
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build the Java simulation
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run the import workflow demo
java -cp target/classes com.bank.iac.TerraformImportDemo

# The real Terraform workflow this simulates:
cd terraform
terraform init
# Terraform 1.5+ generates a starting config from the import block:
terraform plan -generate-config-out=generated.tf
# Review generated.tf, strip computed/noise attrs, move values into variables.tf
terraform plan      # iterate until this shows: "No changes."
terraform apply     # applies the import, adopting the bucket into state
git add main.tf variables.tf && git commit -m "Adopt legacy audit bucket into Terraform"
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input: a real S3 bucket `nbi-audit-logs-prod` with versioning Enabled, AES256 encryption, and tag team=compliance, plus an engineer who writes minimal HCL that only mentions the bucket name and the team tag.

Step 1: The engineer authors a minimal `aws_s3_bucket.audit` block. At this point the config exists on disk but Terraform state has no entry for it, so a naive apply would try to create a duplicate.

Step 2: The engineer runs import, which binds the address `aws_s3_bucket.audit` to the live ID `nbi-audit-logs-prod` inside the state file. The config on disk is untouched — import wrote to state only, nothing else changed.

Step 3: The first plan compares the engineer's config against the live bucket. Because the config never mentioned versioning or encryption, Terraform believes those should be absent and proposes to remove them. The plan is dirty with two unexpected changes. The data that changed is the engineer's understanding; the real bucket and the state are stable.

Step 4: The engineer reads the plan and adds the versioning Enabled block and the AES256 encryption block to the HCL. The config on disk now matches reality.

Step 5: The second plan compares again and finds no differences. The plan is clean. Only now is it safe to commit the HCL to version control, because a clean plan proves config, state, and reality all agree.

```
2026-10-30 01:30:11 [INFO   ] National Bank of India — adopting legacy audit bucket into Terraform

2026-10-30 01:30:11 [WARNING] PLAN: 2 unexpected change(s) — config does NOT yet match live. Iterate!
2026-10-30 01:30:11 [WARNING]   ~ sse_algorithm: will REMOVE live value 'AES256' (config is silent)
2026-10-30 01:30:11 [WARNING]   ~ versioning: will REMOVE live value 'Enabled' (config is silent)
2026-10-30 01:30:11 [INFO   ] Second plan after iterating on config:
2026-10-30 01:30:11 [INFO   ] PLAN: No changes. Config matches live resource. Safe to commit.

  │ STATE: aws_s3_bucket.audit -> nbi-audit-logs-prod │

            │                         │
            ▼                         ▼

```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Bringing an existing or legacy AWS resource under Terraform management is a deliberate four-step workflow, and the single most important thing to understand is that importing only edits Terraform's state file — it never writes your configuration for you. First I author HCL that I believe matches the live resource. Second I run terraform import, which binds my resource address to the real object's import ID inside state, so Terraform stops trying to create a duplicate. Third I run terraform plan and read every proposed change line by line. Fourth I iterate on my HCL, copying the real settings the plan is complaining about, until the plan reports no changes, and only then do I commit.

The reason import does not produce clean config is that import is a one-way read into state; it has no opinion about how your HCL should look. Even the newer generate-config-out feature, which does scaffold HCL, produces noisy output full of computed and default attributes that I still have to strip, and I still have to replace hardcoded values with variables and group resources into modules so the config is reusable and reviewable.

In my project at the National Bank of India, a contractor had manually created an S3 bucket called nbi-audit-logs-prod that stored transaction audit logs for accounts like Rajesh's SAV2001 and Priya's CUR3001, complete with versioning and AES-256 encryption. I wrote a minimal resource block, imported the bucket into state, and the very first plan tried to strip versioning and encryption because my config had not mentioned them. I read that plan, added the versioning and encryption blocks, moved the bucket name into a variable, and iterated until the plan was silent. Only a clean plan proves that my configuration, Terraform's state, and the real infrastructure all agree, and that is the exact moment adoption is safe to commit. The discipline I always emphasise is that a clean plan — not a successful import — is the finish line.
